Chapter Two: The Power of Myth and the Wisdom Hidden in Old Stories
There’s just something about those old stories, isn’t there?
They tend to linger, quietly echoing in the background, long after we’ve heard the last word. Myths and fairy tales—especially the ones that have lasted for centuries—they aren’t just about entertainment. They’re layered with meaning, slipping past our usual defenses and speaking to the deeper parts of ourselves that daily life often ignores.
In many ways, they serve as a kind of roadmap for our inner journeys, especially when it comes to growing up—from boyhood into manhood.
Take the story of Iron John.
On the surface, it looks like a simple fairy tale—a wild man, a curious prince, and a bunch of trials and transformations. But if you look beneath the surface, you’ll see it’s really about the challenges every man faces as he grows up.
The wild man, with his tangled hair and fierce eyes, stands for the parts of us that are powerful, unpredictable, and, let’s be honest, a little scary. Meanwhile, the young prince, drawn to that mysterious cage, is all about the longing to break free from childhood and find out who we really are.
Most people don’t realize just how much these old stories shape the way they see the world. Even if we forget the details, the patterns stick around. The journey into the forest, bumping up against the unknown, facing tests and trials—these are all part of growing up.
Back in the day, communities used to mark these transitions with rituals and ceremonies. Boys would be taken from their families, taught the skills and values they needed to become men, and then welcomed back as adults.
Those rites of passage were more than just tradition—they honored the real changes that come with maturity.
But today, most of those rituals have vanished.
Boys grow up surrounded by distractions—TV, video games, packed schedules—but rarely face real challenges.
The old journey into the forest has been replaced by a kind of wandering, a search for meaning that often just leads to feeling lost or unsure.
But here’s where the wisdom of myth comes in.
It shows us that the path to manhood isn’t just about being tough or independent.
It’s about facing the wild, untamed sides of ourselves and figuring out how to bring them into our everyday lives.
The wild man in Iron John isn’t just some scary figure—he’s also a source of strength, creativity, and deep emotion. By freeing the wild man, the young prince starts to discover those same qualities inside himself.
Think about this: one man looked back on his life and realized he’d spent years trying to fit in, doing everything “right,” but still felt empty.
It wasn’t until he started exploring old stories—reading about heroes, monsters, magical helpers—that he saw his struggles in a new light.
The stories didn’t hand him easy answers, but they helped him see that his longing for something more was actually part of a much older pattern.
Another man, wrestling with addiction, found comfort in thinking of his journey as a kind of initiation.
The setbacks and failures weren’t just flaws—they were steps in the larger process of transformation.
The story of Iron John, with all its ups and downs, gave him hope that even the darkest moments could eventually lead to growth.
That’s the power of myth—it speaks to the whole person, not just the mind, but the heart and soul too.
It reminds us that the path to maturity is both universal and deeply personal. Each man has to find his own way, but these old stories offer guidance, encouragement, and a sense of belonging. They suggest that the wildness inside us isn’t something to fear or suppress, but something to honor and weave into our lives.
In a world that often pushes us to fit in and go with the flow, the wisdom found in myth matters more than ever. It calls us back to those deeper currents of life, to the real challenges and joys of becoming fully human.
The story of Iron John, with all its danger and possibility, becomes a touchstone for anyone willing to take that journey.
It’s a gentle but powerful reminder that the road to manhood isn’t straight—it winds through darkness and difficulty, but also leads to strength, connection, and finally, a sense of home.
